method: Scope was assigned only where a complete inspected document or a publisher, journal, or university abstract stated the work's actual treatment. Titles alone were not treated as sufficient evidence.
policy: These notes support work-level scope classification only. They make no claim about complete object extraction, preferred readings, identity, rights, or permission to reproduce text or images.

entries.finding: The complete 97-page file is a commercial auction catalogue presenting sale conditions and numbered lots. Its three bowl lots are market descriptions, not a scholarly edition or study.

entries.finding: The complete article comments on and corrects readings across a published corpus, then presents two new bowls and a revised edition of a third bowl in its appendices.
The complete working list enumerates forty-one published Syriac 'Manichaean' bowls and separately notes related candidates; it is an object-and-publication catalogue rather than an edition.
The complete article gives first editions of two previously unpublished Syriac incantation texts, one bowl and one British Museum fragment.
The Oxford University Press abstract states that the article publishes a new NLI bowl in full and re-examines three parallel Penn bowls, including a full edition of B16041.

The article abstract frames the work as an onomastic and philological investigation of the divine name YHBYH across the bowl corpus, its relation to the Tetragrammaton, and its pluriconfessional setting.
The abstract states that the article provides a transcription, translation and analysis of one unpublished Penn Museum bowl, B9002.
The Oxford University Press abstract identifies the article as the editio princeps of five Mandaic bowls in the Abgine Museum.
The abstract describes a study of three parallels between the Babylonian Talmud and incantation bowls to investigate textual circulation and reworking, not an edition of those objects.
The Hebrew University record identifies a peer-reviewed article focused on authorship, agency and gender in incantation-bowl formulae rather than an object edition.
The author abstract says the article examines references to Moses in the bowls, including scribal authority, self-identification, scriptural episodes and possible imagery.
The Utrecht University abstract describes a study of gender terminology, beneficiaries and creators across the Mesopotamian bowl corpus.
The Oxford University Press abstract states that the article presents the first publication and contextual discussion of one bowl, MC 77.233.
The University of Milano-Bicocca repository abstract describes the work as the editio princeps of one Aramaic incantation bowl, IM 77781.
The Hebrew University record identifies a social-historical study using the bowl corpus as evidence for Babylonian Jewish society, not an edition.
